steps.prompt: How fast is this code, really?
steps.sub: AI hands you a 'clever' solution in three seconds. Looks fine. Runs on the example. But will it survive a million-row input — or quietly time out? By the end of this you'll read the cost off any solution at a glance, and catch O(n²) wearing a clever disguise.

steps.prompt: First instinct — what does Big-O actually measure?

options.t: How many seconds the code takes to run on your laptop.
How the work (time or memory) GROWS as the input gets bigger.
How many lines of code the solution has.

steps.why: Big-O is about GROWTH, not stopwatch seconds. Your laptop's speed, the language, the weather — none of that matters. O(n) means 'double the input, roughly double the work.' O(n²) means 'double the input, 4× the work.' That shape is what decides whether you survive a million rows.
hints: Two of these depend on your specific machine or your typing. Big-O ignores both.
It answers: when the input gets 10× bigger, how much MORE work happens?

steps.prompt: The five costs you'll meet 95% of the time.
steps.sub: Tap each card. Memorise the shape, not the math.

cards.b: Same work no matter the size. Hash-map lookup, array index. The dream.
Halve the problem each step. Binary search on a sorted array. A million items → ~20 steps.
Touch each item once. A single for-loop over the input. Usually 'good enough'.
The speed limit for sorting/comparison. A clean nested-ish solution. This is your target on most array problems.
A loop INSIDE a loop over the same data. Fine for n=100, a disaster at n=1,000,000. The classic interview trap.

steps.prompt: Read each code shape — which cost is it?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then a bin. This is the operator's core reflex.

items.t: one for-loop summing every element once
a for-loop, and inside it ANOTHER for-loop over the same array
binary search: halve the range each step
scan the array once, storing seen values in a hash set
for each element, scan all the others to find a pair
sort the array, then walk it once

hints: A loop nested inside another loop over the SAME n is the quadratic tell.
Sorting is O(n log n). 'Halve it each step' is the log signature.

steps.prompt: AI gives you this for 'find the two numbers that sum to target': for each number, loop through all the others looking for its partner. It passes the example. Your move?
steps.sub: You're the operator reviewing the agent's work.

options.t: Ship it — it returns the correct answer on the test case.
Flag it: that's a loop-in-a-loop, O(n²). Ask for a hash-map version that's O(n).
Rewrite the whole thing in a faster language.

steps.why: Correctness on one example is the floor, not the finish line. 'For each, scan the rest' is the textbook O(n²) pattern. The operator's move: recognise it instantly and redirect — 'use a hash set of seen values, check target − x in one pass.' That's O(n). Same answer, survives a million inputs.
hints: Correct ≠ efficient. What's the COST shape of 'for each, scan all the others'?
A 'have I seen its partner?' question is exactly what a hash set makes O(1).

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: O(2n) and O(n) are treated as the same complexity.
statements.why: Yes — Big-O drops constant factors. 2n, 5n, 100n are all O(n). We care about the SHAPE of growth, not the multiplier.

statements.t: An O(n²) solution is always too slow to use.
statements.why: No — for small, bounded n (say n ≤ 1000) O(n²) is perfectly fine and often simpler. The danger is only when n can be large. Knowing the input size is part of the judgment.

statements.t: Time complexity is the only thing that matters; you can ignore memory.
statements.why: No — space complexity counts too. The hash-map trick trades O(n) extra memory for speed. Interviewers love asking 'can you do it with O(1) space?'

statements.t: On a sorted input, you should suspect a faster-than-linear solution exists.
statements.why: Right — 'sorted' is a giant hint. It usually unlocks binary search O(log n) or two-pointers O(n), beating the brute-force O(n²).

hints: Big-O keeps the growth shape and throws away constants.
Think about WHEN a slow-looking solution is actually acceptable.

steps.prompt: Walk a real review: AI just sent you a solution. Decide each move.
steps.sub: You're under interview pressure. The interviewer is watching you read the cost.
steps.goal: Approve only an efficient, correct solution to 'does this array have any duplicates?'

turns.situation: AI's first attempt: two nested loops comparing every pair of elements.
turns.q: What do you say out loud first?
options: "This is O(n²) — for each element it scans the rest. Let's improve it."
turns.log: 🔍 Spotted: nested loops over same array → O(n²).

turns.situation: You ask for a better approach. The interviewer nods.
turns.q: What do you direct the agent toward?
options: A hash set: add each element, return true the moment you see a repeat
Sorting it three times to be safe
turns.log: 🧠 Direct → 'use a seen-set, O(n) time, O(n) space.'

turns.situation: AI returns the hash-set version. It passes the example.
turns.q: Before approving, what's your last check?
options: Confirm the complexity AND an edge case (empty array, all-same)
Ask it to rewrite in assembly
turns.log: ✅ O(n) verified + edge cases checked. Approved.

hints: The operator names the cost before touching the keyboard.
Final gate = complexity is right AND the edge cases hold.

steps.prompt: Put the operator's review loop in order.
steps.sub: This is the habit that makes you look senior in any interview.
chips: Read the code and name its Big-O
Decide if that cost is acceptable for the input size
Direct a faster approach if it's not
Verify correctness + edge cases before approving
hints: You can't judge 'acceptable' until you've named the cost.
Naming the cost comes first; verifying correctness is the final gate.

steps.prompt: Why must YOU read the complexity off the agent's code, instead of trusting it?
steps.sub: This is the whole reason complexity still matters in the AI era.

options.t: Because AI never writes correct code.
Because AI optimises for 'looks plausible and passes the example' — it'll happily hand you an O(n²) solution dressed as clever, and only your eye catches it before it ships.
Because reading Big-O is required by company policy.

steps.why: AI is a fast, confident pattern-matcher — not a guarantee of efficiency. It often produces correct-but-slow code that sails through the happy path. In the interview AND on the job, you are the reviewer: the value you add is the eye that reads the cost and redirects. That's the operator's mindset this whole course is built on.
hints: Think about what 'passes the example' does and doesn't prove.
If AI writes the code, what is the human now paid to do?

steps.sub: Not graded. Tie this to the remote SWE job you're chasing.

fields.label: What kind of remote SWE role are you targeting (so we tune examples to it)?
fields.ph: e.g. backend Python, full-stack React, data engineering

fields.label: Write your one-line complexity reflex — the question you'll ask of every AI solution from now on:
fields.ph: e.g. "What's the Big-O, and is that OK for my input size?"
